title: Salaam & Respect
tagline: Greet elders, say how you are, and never call Nani 'tu'.
canDo: You can greet anyone in the family with the right level of respect

grammar.title: hai, hain, ho, hoon
grammar.body: The verb 'to be' changes with who you're talking about: main … hoon (I am), tum … ho (you are, casual), aap … hain (you are, respectful), yeh/woh … hai (he/she/it is). Respectful always takes the plural form hain, even for one person.

grammar.title: aap, tum, tu
grammar.body: Three words for 'you'. aap: elders, strangers, in-laws, anyone you'd be scared to disappoint. tum: friends, cousins, younger people. tu: God, tiny children, your closest friend… or someone you're about to fight. When unsure, aap. Nobody was ever disowned for being too polite.

phrases.note: Stick ji on anything to make it polite: Khala ji, ji haan, ji shukriya.

phrases.en: How are you? (respectful, to a man)
How are you? (respectful, to a woman)

phrases.note: The default answer to 'how are you' in most Pakistani homes.

phrases.en: How are you? (casual, to a guy)
How are you? (casual, to a girl)
How are you? (intimate, to a guy)

phrases.note: Works as 'thank you' and, with a request, as 'please'.
The Swiss Army knife of Urdu. Tone does all the work.

phrases.roman: aap se mil kar khushi hui
phrases.urdu: آپ سے مل کر خوشی ہوئی
accept: aap se mil ke khushi hui

phrases.note: Elders call every younger person beta, girls included. You are 'beta' until you are about 50.
Nobody leaves a Pakistani house without being handed a salaam to deliver.
From a parent, 'Inshallah' can mean anything from 'definitely' to 'absolutely not'.
You'll hear this, not say it. The right reply is a small smile and lowered eyes.

phrases.roman: Main theek hoon. Aap kaisi hain?
phrases.urdu: میں ٹھیک ہوں۔ آپ کیسی ہیں؟
accept: main theek hoon aap kaisi hain
main theek hoon shukriya aap kaisi hain

phrases.en: How are you? (intimate. To your KHALA.)
Sorry! How are YOU? (respectfully this time)

phrases.roman: Achha beta, Ammi ko salaam kehna
phrases.urdu: اچھا بیٹا، امی کو سلام کہنا
phrases.en: Okay dear, say salaam to your mum
phrases.speaker: khala

phrases.urdu: ان شاء اللہ۔ اللہ حافظ خالہ جی

lessons.title: Salaam
lessons.blurb: The first ten seconds at any desi door.
lessons.canDo: You can give and return a proper salaam

teach.tip: The universal opener. Say it first, say it to elders, say it even if you were just in the room two minutes ago.
The reply. Skipping it is how you end up as a topic at the next family dinner.
The short version, for cousins and people your own age.
Your new best friend. 'Ji' means yes, and also turns anything respectful: Khala ji, Abbu ji.
Thank you. You'll need it: someone is about to hand you chai.

exercises.prompt: Nani says “Assalam-o-alaikum”. You say:
exercises.explain: A salaam gets 'walaikum assalam' back. Always.

exercises.prompt: You walk into a room with Nani, two uncles and your cousin Bilal. Who do you salaam first?

options.feedback: Correct. Bilal can wait. Bilal can always wait.
Nani saw that. Nani sees everything.
A wave. In front of Nani. Brave.

exercises.explain: Greet the eldest person first. One loud 'Assalam-o-alaikum' to the whole room also works.

exercises.prompt: Khala opens the door. Type your greeting.
She salaams you back first. Build your reply.
Khala hands you chai. Type: “Thank you”

lessons.title: Kya haal hai?
lessons.blurb: Ask how someone is. Answer without saying 'good, you?'
lessons.canDo: You can ask an elder how they are and answer when they ask you

teach.tip: To a man you respect. 'Aap' is the polite you; 'hain' goes with it.
To a woman. Only one sound changes: kaise → kaisi.
Works for everyone, any gender. The safe option when your brain freezes.
'Theek' = fine, okay. You'll say it 40 times a day.
What most people actually answer. It means you're fine without you having to commit to any details.
Always bounce the question back. It's just manners.

exercises.prompt: You're greeting Shabnam Khala (your aunt). Ask how she is.
exercises.explain: Khala is a woman, so kaisi.

exercises.prompt: Now ask Abbu (your dad) how he is.
exercises.explain: Abbu is a man, so kaise.
main … hoon. 'I' always ends in hoon.

exercises.prompt: Khala: “Kya haal hai, beta?” Tell her you're fine.
Uncle asks “Kya haal hai?” You are, in fact, exhausted and behind on everything. What do you say?

options.feedback: Correct. Nobody asked for the real answer.
He has already started walking to the samosas.

exercises.explain: 'Kya haal hai?' is a greeting, not a medical intake form.

exercises.prompt: You've said you're fine. Now bounce it back: “And you?”

lessons.title: Aap, tum, tu
lessons.blurb: Three ways to say 'you'. One of them can end a dinner.
lessons.canDo: You can pick aap, tum or tu for the person in front of you

teach.title: Urdu has three 'you's
teach.info: English lost 'thou' centuries ago. Urdu kept everything. Which 'you' you pick tells the listener exactly how much you respect them, so choose wisely.

teach.tip: Elders, strangers, in-laws, teachers, your friend's parents. The verb ends in 'hain'.
Friends, cousins your age, younger siblings. The verb ends in 'ho'.
Best friends, small children, God, and people you are yelling at in traffic. The verb ends in 'hai'.
Same question, casual. Notice aap…hain became tum…ho.

teach.title: Elders say tum. You still say aap.
teach.info: Khala will call you 'tum' or 'beta'. That is not an invitation to say 'tum' back. Respect in Urdu flows uphill only.

exercises.situation: Nani opens the door. You want to ask how she is.

options.feedback: Perfect. Nani nods, almost imperceptibly. High praise.
Tum? To Nani? She's not angry. She's disappointed. That's worse.
Tu to Nani?? Bold choice. Your mother has been informed.

exercises.situation: Your cousin Bilal (same age, insufferable) walks in.

options.feedback: Exactly right for a cousin your own age.
Works, but 'aap' to Bilal will go straight to his head. He's a doctor, he has enough ego.
Fine if you two are close. If not, that's fighting talk.

exercises.explain: tum … ho. aap … hain. main … hoon.
aap always takes hain, even when you're talking to just one person.

exercises.prompt: Khala says to you: “Tum kaise ho, beta?” What do you call HER when you answer?

options.feedback: Yes. She can 'tum' you. You 'aap' her. Forever.
It's not a mirror. Respect flows uphill only.
We'll pretend that didn't happen.

exercises.situation: A rickshaw driver you've never met. You want to ask how he is.

options.feedback: Aap for strangers, always. Also he sets the fare, so be nice.
People do say 'tum' to drivers. Those people are being rude. Don't be those people.
The fare just doubled.

exercises.prompt: Text your (male) cousin: “How are you?” Casual.
Now ask your friend's dad the same thing. Respectfully.

lessons.title: Ji haan, ji nahin
lessons.blurb: Yes, no, thanks, sorry, and the mighty 'achha'.
lessons.canDo: You can say yes, no, thank you and sorry politely

teach.tip: Polite yes. Just 'ji' works too, and is what you'll mumble most.
Polite no. Will not actually stop anyone putting more rice on your plate.
'Bohat' = very, a lot. Add it to anything.
A warmer, more old-school thank-you. Aunties love it.
Sorry or excuse me. For stepping on feet and interrupting gossip.
The gracious reply to an apology.
Achha. (Okay.) Achha? (Really?) Achhaaa. (I see.) ACHHA. (Enough.) One word, infinite meanings.

exercises.prompt: Abbu: “Did you pray?” Answer yes, politely.
exercises.explain: 'Haan' alone is fine with friends. With Abbu, add ji.

exercises.prompt: Your cousin apologises for spilling chai on you. Be gracious.
Nani slips you Eidi money. Type: “Thank you very much”
Khala: “Aur chawal?” (More rice?) You are extremely full. You say “Ji nahin, shukriya.” What happens?

options.text: She puts more rice on your plate anyway
options.feedback: Correct. 'Nahin' is treated as an opening bid.
Adorable. No.

exercises.explain: You'll learn the real defence ('bas, bas!') in Dawat Survival.

exercises.prompt: You bump into an uncle at the wedding buffet. Apologise.
Rishta Aunty: “Beta, are you married?” Type a polite no.

lessons.title: Aap ka naam?
lessons.blurb: Names, introductions, and why everyone calls you 'beta'.
lessons.canDo: You can introduce yourself and your parents

teach.tip: 'Aap ka' = your (respectful). Naam = name. Easy one.
'Mera' = my. Swap in your own name. The verb goes last: my name Ali is.
Long, but it makes aunties melt. Worth the effort.
'Yeh' = this, 'kaun' = who. 'Hain' because you're being respectful about them.
'Meri' for a woman…
…and 'mere' for a man you respect. Yes, 'my' changes too. Urdu is thorough.
Means 'son', but elders say it to everyone younger. A stranger aunty calling you beta is normal. Enjoy it.

exercises.prompt: An aunty you've never seen asks your name. (Today you're Ali.)

exercises.explain: Ammi is a woman, so meri.
For a man you respect it's mere (the respectful plural), not mera.

exercises.prompt: Introduce yourself as Ali.
You've just met your friend's grandmother. Say the nice thing.
A total stranger at the shop calls you “beta”. What's going on?

options.text: Nothing. Every elder calls every younger person beta.
options.feedback: Exactly. You have roughly 4,000 honorary aunties and uncles.
She does not. But she will still ask if you've eaten.

exercises.prompt: Ask your new neighbour, an uncle, his name.

lessons.title: Khuda hafiz
lessons.blurb: The desi goodbye: 45 minutes, starts at the door.
lessons.canDo: You can say goodbye properly (and survive the long version)

teach.tip: The classic goodbye.
Just as common. Use whichever your family uses.
'Phir' = again. A warm way to close.
'Khayal' = care, thought. The '-iye' ending makes it respectful.
You will be given salaams to deliver. Delivering them is not optional.
Attach to any plan. 'Phir milenge, Inshallah.'
An elder's blessing as you leave. You don't say it back; you just glow.

exercises.prompt: You're leaving Nani's house. Tell her to take care, respectfully.
exercises.explain: 'Jeete raho' is what SHE says to YOU.

exercises.prompt: Type a goodbye. (Either common one works.)
Nani says “Jeete raho, beta.” What do you say back?

options.feedback: Right. It's a blessing. You receive it.
You just told your grandmother to live long, like she's a child. She's laughing. You're lucky.

exercises.prompt: Khala is seeing you off. What does she tell you?
Type: “See you again”
Khala: “Come again next week!” Give the classic non-committal answer.

lessons.title: Mix it up
lessons.blurb: Everything from this unit, shuffled. Warm-up for the boss.
lessons.canDo: You can use this unit's phrases without a prompt: you can greet anyone in the family with the right level of respect

teach.title: Boss warm-up
teach.info: Everything from this unit, mixed together and mostly production: you say it, you type it. Mistakes come back, as always, for free.

exercises.prompt: What's the word for “Hello”?
Type the word for “Thank you”
Type the word for “you”
Type it: “No”
Nani is waiting. Say: “No problem / never mind”
Type the word for “dear / kiddo”

boss.title: The Doorway
boss.blurb: Shabnam Khala opens the door. Get through the greeting alive.
boss.scene: You're standing outside Shabnam Khala's house holding a box of mithai. The door swings open before you can knock. She was watching from the window.
boss.canDo: You can get through a full doorstep greeting with an elder

options.reaction: The 'ji' did not go unnoticed. She's already telling people you're 'such a well-raised child'.
A bare 'salaam' to your Khala. She lets it slide. This time.

y2.prompt: Say you're fine, and ask about her.

options.reaction: Solid. Though she noticed you didn't ask how SHE is.

oops.text: Record scratch. The whole house goes quiet. Somewhere inside, Nani puts down her chai.

options.reaction: Crisis averted. She will still bring this up at your wedding.
No apology, but the 'aap' is back. She'll take it.

y3.prompt: Tell her your mum is fine.

y4.prompt: Thank her as you step inside.

options.reaction: 'Meherbani'! She clutches her dupatta. Who taught you that?

later.text: Three hours, four cups of chai and one interrogation about your career later, you're back at the door.

y5.prompt: Accept the mission and say goodbye.

options.reaction: 'Inshallah' for delivering a salaam. Non-committal to the end.

end.title: You survived the doorway
end.text: Greeting, small talk, goodbye: done, in Urdu, with an elder. Khala has already called your mum to report that you 'speak so nicely now'.
